description: Process lifecycle decomposed. fork's COW + fd inheritance + signal-handler-reset semantics. exec's image replacement. wait/waitpid + zombies. Signal handling around fork. posix_spawn as the modern alternative. The fork-exec pattern + its modern alternatives.

sub_mechanisms.name: fork_copy_on_write
sub_mechanisms.definition: fork() doesn't actually copy memory; marks both processes' pages as read-only. First write triggers fault → kernel allocates a private copy.
sub_mechanisms.why: Cheap fork even for large processes. Cost only paid for pages actually modified. Most modern apps that fork+exec never modify memory in the child (exec replaces it). Effective zero-cost fork in common case.

sub_mechanisms.name: fork_fd_inheritance
sub_mechanisms.definition: Child inherits parent's open file descriptors. fd table is copied; underlying file descriptions are shared.
sub_mechanisms.why: Foundation of pipe-based pipelines: parent creates pipe, forks, child has both ends. Allows fds to be set up before exec. CLOEXEC flag on fd marks it for closing on exec.

sub_mechanisms.name: fork_signal_state
sub_mechanisms.definition: Child inherits parent's signal handlers but pending signals are not inherited. Signal mask is preserved.
sub_mechanisms.why: Predictable signal behavior: handlers set up in parent are active in child. Pending signals not inherited prevents accidental double-delivery. Standard POSIX semantics.

sub_mechanisms.name: exec_image_replacement
sub_mechanisms.definition: execve loads a new program into the calling process: replaces text + heap + stack + memory mappings. PID + fds (without CLOEXEC) preserved.
sub_mechanisms.why: Clean transition from one program to another in the same process. Lets a parent set up the environment (cwd, fds, env vars), then exec the desired program. fork+exec is the Unix idiom for spawning.

sub_mechanisms.name: CLOEXEC_flag
sub_mechanisms.definition: Per-fd flag: if set, the fd is closed automatically on exec. Set via open(O_CLOEXEC) or fcntl(F_SETFD, FD_CLOEXEC).
sub_mechanisms.why: Prevents fd leaks across exec: child shouldn't inherit fds the parent uses internally. Best practice: open with O_CLOEXEC by default. Pre-CLOEXEC, manual fcntl was required (race conditions on threaded programs).

sub_mechanisms.name: wait_exit_status
sub_mechanisms.definition: wait/waitpid returns child's exit status: 8-bit exit code (from main return or exit()) or signal that killed it.
sub_mechanisms.why: Parent's communication channel with child completion. WIFEXITED + WEXITSTATUS macros interpret. Bash's $? captures this. waitpid's WNOHANG flag enables non-blocking polling.

sub_mechanisms.name: orphan_process
sub_mechanisms.definition: Process whose parent has exited. Reparented to init (PID 1) which waits for it.
sub_mechanisms.why: Prevents zombies when parents die first. init is responsible for reaping orphans. In containers, the PID-1 process plays this role (problems if it doesn't, hence tini, dumb-init).

sub_mechanisms.name: double_fork_daemon_pattern
sub_mechanisms.definition: Daemonisation: fork; in child setsid + fork again; in grandchild do work. Original parent reaped by init via the intermediate child's exit.
sub_mechanisms.why: Grandchild is fully detached: no session, no terminal, reaped by init. Without double fork, daemon could acquire a controlling TTY (unwanted). Modern systemd handles daemon setup; manual double-fork persists in legacy code.

sub_mechanisms.name: process_credentials
sub_mechanisms.definition: Per-process UID/GID + supplementary groups + effective/real/saved variants. Determine permission for file access + syscalls.
sub_mechanisms.why: User identity carried through process tree. setuid/setgid syscalls change them (with restrictions). suid bit on executables runs the program as the file's owner.

sub_mechanisms.name: posix_spawn
sub_mechanisms.definition: Single syscall combining fork + exec atomically. posix_spawn(&pid, path, file_actions, attrp, argv, envp).
sub_mechanisms.why: Avoids fork's COW cost when child immediately execs (the common case). On Linux, posix_spawn uses vfork-style optimisation internally. Faster + simpler than fork+exec for spawn use cases.

sub_mechanisms.name: vfork
sub_mechanisms.definition: Legacy syscall: like fork but child shares parent's address space. Parent suspended until child execs or exits.
sub_mechanisms.why: Avoid COW page table setup. Dangerous: child can corrupt parent's memory. Mostly superseded by posix_spawn + Linux's optimised fork. Used in some embedded contexts.

sub_mechanisms.name: clone_syscall
sub_mechanisms.definition: Linux-specific: like fork but with fine-grained control over what's shared (memory, fds, signal handlers, etc.). The underlying primitive for pthread + container creation.
sub_mechanisms.why: Same syscall for: thread (share everything), container (new namespaces), process (share little). Flag bits control sharing per resource. fork is clone with default flags; pthread_create is clone with CLONE_VM|CLONE_FILES|CLONE_THREAD.

derivation_rules.name: COW_makes_fork_cheap_when_child_execs
if: child immediately calls exec without writing memory
then: fork's cost is just the page table copy
derivation_rules.why: No actual page copies. Page table setup is O(memory size in PTEs) — for typical processes, hundreds of μs. The 'COW + exec' idiom is what makes Unix process creation tractable.

derivation_rules.name: posix_spawn_beats_fork_exec_when_combined
if: fork is immediately followed by exec
derivation_rules.why: fork sets up COW for memory that exec immediately discards. posix_spawn skips the COW setup. On large processes (modern JVMs, browsers), the difference is dramatic. Modern Python's subprocess uses posix_spawn when possible.

derivation_rules.name: wait_required_to_prevent_zombies
if: a process forks children but never waits
derivation_rules.why: Exited but unwaited children stay in the process table holding only PID + exit status. Each is tiny but they exhaust PIDs. Long-running daemons must wait or SIGCHLD-handle correctly.

derivation_rules.name: CLOEXEC_prevents_fd_leak_to_child
if: a file descriptor is marked CLOEXEC
derivation_rules.why: Without CLOEXEC, all fds the parent had open are visible to the child. Security risk (child could access parent's resources) + resource leak (file remains open). Best practice: open with O_CLOEXEC by default.

derivation_rules.name: clone_unifies_threading_and_process_creation
if: fork is clone with default flags and pthread_create is clone with shared flags
then: the OS treats threading + forking as a single primitive
derivation_rules.why: Linux's clone exposes all the sharing dimensions. fork: share nothing (process). pthread_create: share memory/fds/signal handlers (thread). Containers: share or unshare namespaces. One mechanism, many use cases.
